q: A hybrid project must meet a fixed regulatory date, while its software streams work in sprints. How does the PMBOK Guide suggest structuring its schedule?
options: One detailed critical path schedule for all the work
Predictive milestones, with sprints inside them
Only sprints, with no milestones at all
A Kanban board for the whole project
explanation: In a hybrid approach, the high-level schedule uses predictive techniques to outline key milestones and deliverables; within it, streams use adaptive iterations, Kanban or the critical path method.

q: Where would the team record the release and iteration length, the units of measure and the schedule control thresholds?
options: The project charter document
The resource calendar
The milestone list
The schedule management plan
explanation: The schedule management plan covers schedule development, release and iteration length, level of accuracy, units of measure, organizational links, maintenance, control thresholds, performance measurement rules and reporting formats.

q: Testing can begin three days after coding begins, as soon as the first module is ready. How should the scheduler model this?
options: Start-to-start with a 3-day lag
Finish-to-start with a 3-day lead
Finish-to-finish with a 3-day lag
Start-to-finish with no lag
explanation: The successor (testing) can start only after the predecessor (coding) has started, delayed by three days: a start-to-start relationship with a 3-day lag.
ref: PMBOK 8, Guide section 5, Leads and lags

links.label: PMBOK 8, Guide section 5, Leads and lags

q: The city must grant a road-works permit before excavation can begin, and the team cannot speed the permit up. How is this dependency classified?
options: Discretionary and internal
Discretionary and external
Mandatory and external
Mandatory and internal
explanation: It is required (mandatory) and depends on a non-project activity outside the team's control (external). The Eighth Edition notes that two attributes apply at once, for example a mandatory external dependency.
ref: PMBOK 8, Guide section 5, Dependency determination and integration

links.label: PMBOK 8, Guide section 5, Dependency determination and integration

q: To fast track a late schedule, which dependencies should the project manager review first for possible change?
options: Mandatory dependencies set by the nature of the work
Discretionary dependencies chosen as preferred logic
External dependencies on government approvals
Leads and lags written into the contracts
explanation: Discretionary dependencies are preferred logic. They should be fully documented and, when fast tracking, reviewed and considered for modification or removal.

q: A scheduler adds a 10-day lag in place of a missing logical link, so that the dates look right. What is wrong with this?
options: Lags must always be shown as negative values
Lags may be used only on finish-to-finish links
A lag over five days needs the sponsor's approval
Leads and lags should not replace schedule logic
explanation: The team decides which dependencies need a lead or lag to define the logic accurately, but leads and lags should not replace schedule logic, and duration estimates do not include them.
ref: PMBOK 8, Guide section 5, Leads and lags

links.label: PMBOK 8, Guide section 5, Leads and lags

q: The customer's approval of the design must appear in the schedule. How should the scheduler model it?
options: As a milestone with zero duration
As a five-day activity with resources
As a lag on the design activity
As a note in the risk register
explanation: A milestone has zero duration and no resources. It marks the start or completion of a deliverable and may reflect external constraints, such as a required approval.

q: Who should provide the inputs for an activity's duration estimate, according to the PMBOK Guide?
options: The sponsor, since they fund the work
The average of all estimates given
The people most familiar with the work
The most optimistic estimate offered
explanation: The inputs for duration estimates come from the person or group on the team most familiar with the nature of the work for that activity.

q: A 24-hour stress test is on the critical path. The sponsor wants more testers added to shorten it. What should the project manager say?
options: Doubling testers will halve the duration
The test's duration is fixed by its nature
Crashing always works on critical activities
Fast tracking it will remove the risk
explanation: Some work takes a set time whatever the resources, such as a 24-hour stress test. Crashing works only where added resources actually shorten the activity.

q: A team's estimates are always too optimistic, although its members know that similar past work ran late. Which bias does the PMBOK Guide name for this?
options: Law of diminishing returns
Resource leveling
Free float
Planning fallacy
explanation: Cognitive biases such as the planning fallacy and end-of-story illusion, and phenomena like Hofstadter's law, can reduce the accuracy of scheduling.

q: Estimates for an activity are 6 days optimistic, 9 most likely and 18 pessimistic. The PMO uses the beta (PERT) formula. By how many days does the expected duration exceed the most likely estimate?
options: 1 day
2 days
0 days
3 days
explanation: Beta: (6 + 4 × 9 + 18) / 6 = 60 / 6 = 10 days, which is 1 day more than the most likely 9. (Triangular would give (6 + 9 + 18) / 3 = 11 days.)

q: A network has three paths: A–B–E takes 18 days, A–C–E 22 days and A–D–E 19 days. Of activities B, C and D, which would delay the project if it slipped by 2 days?
explanation: The longest path, A–C–E (22 days), is critical, so C has zero float (as do A and E). B has 4 days of float and D has 3, so a 2-day slip on either does not move the end date.
ref: PMBOK 8, Guide section 5, Critical path method (CPM)
options: Activity B, on the 18-day path
Activity D, on the 19-day path
Activity C, on the 22-day path
Activity B or D, but not C

links.label: PMBOK 8, Guide section 5, Critical path method (CPM)

q: Using the day-1 convention, an activity finishes early on day 16, and its only successor's early start is day 20. What is the activity's free float?
options: 4 days
3 days
8 days
0 days
explanation: Free float is the time an activity can slip without delaying its successor's early start: 20 − 16 − 1 = 3 days (the successor could start on day 17). In Figure 5-4, B finishes on day 10, D starts on day 16, and B's free float is 5.
ref: PMBOK 8, Guide section 5, Critical path method (CPM)

links.label: PMBOK 8, Guide section 5, Critical path method (CPM)

q: The customer moved the go-live date earlier, and the critical path now shows −3 days of total float. What should the project manager do?
options: Ignore it, since negative float corrects itself later
Remove the go-live constraint from the model
Report that the critical path has disappeared
Use negative float analysis to plan acceleration
explanation: Negative float occurs when constraints force dates earlier than logic and durations allow. Negative float analysis can be used to explore acceleration strategies, such as schedule compression.
ref: PMBOK 8, Guide section 5, Critical path method (CPM)

links.label: PMBOK 8, Guide section 5, Critical path method (CPM)

q: A manager proposes paying overtime to crash an activity that is not on the critical path. What will most likely happen?
options: Cost rises, but the end date does not move
The end date moves earlier by the amount crashed
The critical path shifts to that activity
Risk falls because the work is done sooner
explanation: Crashing works only for activities on the critical path where extra resources shorten the duration. Crashing an activity with float adds cost without shortening the project.

q: The project is two weeks late. The budget is tight, but some risk of rework is acceptable. Which compression technique fits better?
options: Crashing with paid overtime for all
Adding a second contractor crew
Fast tracking two critical activities
Resource smoothing within float
explanation: Fast tracking overlaps activities normally done in sequence; it adds risk and possible rework but not necessarily direct cost. Crashing adds resources and cost. Smoothing does not shorten the schedule.

q: Before the schedule is approved, team members review the dates of their assignments. What are they mainly checking?
options: That their tasks are all on the critical path
That dates fit their other project work
That every activity has a lead or a lag
That the sponsor has signed each task
explanation: Team members confirm that the start and end dates do not conflict with resource calendars or with assignments in other projects or tasks, so the dates are still valid.

q: A program has five projects, and the program board wants to compare their schedules on one page. Which schedule level fits?
options: Level 3, detailed activities
Level 2, managerial view
Level 1, executive summary
Level 0, project summary
explanation: Level 0 is a single line representing the entire project, often used to compare projects in a program or portfolio. Level 1 shows key milestones and summary activities for executives.

q: Operations plans a three-week plant shutdown in July, and the project's installation must happen during it. How should the project manager treat this?
options: As an external dependency to track with operations
As a discretionary dependency that the team can move
As a lag inside the installation activity
As a resource leveling problem
explanation: External dependencies link project activities with non-project activities and are usually outside the team's control. Coordinating with operations is an enabler of the schedule task.

q: When should a project's baseline schedule model be in place?
options: After the first status report
At the end of the first phase
Before the project work begins
Only once a change is requested
explanation: It is generally accepted practice that every project has a baseline schedule model before the work begins. It becomes the benchmark for measuring performance.

q: A major redesign makes the schedule baseline unrealistic. What does the scheduling standard say about rebaselining?
options: Delete the old baseline to avoid any confusion
Agree the causes and archive the original baseline
Keep past variances in the new baseline
Rebaseline monthly to keep the SPI at 1.0
explanation: A rebaseline requires the causes to be identified and agreed by key stakeholders. The original baseline is archived and never deleted; past performance statistics restart from that point.

q: In an agile project, how does Monitor and Control Schedule determine the status of the schedule?
options: By comparing actual dates with the critical path
By counting the hours each member has worked
By the percent complete of every task
By comparing accepted work with the estimate
explanation: With an adaptive approach, status is found by comparing the total work delivered and accepted against the estimates of work completed for the elapsed time cycle.

q: A supplier builds a key component under contract. How does the PMBOK Guide suggest keeping the supplier's work on schedule?
options: Regular and milestone status updates, with reviews
Waiting until delivery, then inspecting the result
Adding the supplier's staff to the project team
Asking the sponsor to call the supplier
explanation: When work is contracted, regular and milestone status updates from contractors and suppliers keep the schedule under control, and scheduled status reviews and walkthroughs check that their reports are accurate.

q: Activity E is now expected to finish 2 days late. What happens to the project's end date?
options: No change, since E has float
It moves 1 day later
It moves 2 days later
It moves 3 days later
explanation: The critical path is B–D–F–G: 5 + 6 + 2 + 3 = 16 days. E is on A–C–E–G: 3 + 4 + 5 + 3 = 15 days, so it has 1 day of float. A 2-day slip uses the float and delays the end by 1 day; A–C–E–G becomes the new critical path at 17 days.
ref: PMBOK 8, Guide section 5, Critical path method (CPM)

links.label: PMBOK 8, Guide section 5, Critical path method (CPM)

q: On a lean construction project, the trades meet to plan the next six weeks together and take on work only when they have capacity. Which method is this?
options: Critical chain
Rolling wave planning
Lean scheduling with pull planning
Location-based scheduling
explanation: Lean scheduling limits queues by pulling work when there is capacity. Team members collaborate in pull-planning sessions; the main steps are master scheduling, phase scheduling and look-ahead planning.

q: Which TWO statements about fast tracking are correct?
options: Activities normally done in sequence overlap
It may cause rework and increase risk
It always lowers the project's cost
It works on activities off the critical path
It adds resources to shorten activities
explanation: Fast tracking performs sequential activities in parallel for part of their duration. It may cause rework, increase risk and need more coordination, and works only when it shortens the critical path. Adding resources is crashing.

q: Which THREE are outputs of the Develop Schedule process?
options: Schedule baseline
Project schedule
Project calendars
Schedule forecasts
Velocity
Stakeholder register
explanation: Figure 2-22 lists the schedule baseline, project schedule, schedule data, project calendars, change requests and updates. Schedule forecasts come from Monitor and Control Schedule.

q: Which TWO does Monitor and Control Schedule do when an agile approach is used?
options: Reprioritize the remaining backlog
Measure velocity in each iteration
Recalculate the critical path every day
Freeze the scope until the release
Rebaseline after every sprint
explanation: In agile, it compares accepted work with the estimate, holds retrospectives, reprioritizes the backlog, measures velocity, and determines and manages schedule changes.

q: Match each scheduling method with how it works.
right: One project buffer protects the due date
Quantities planned by location, crew and rate
Trades pull work in joint planning sessions
Near-term work in detail, later work at high level
explanation: Other approaches named in the Eighth Edition are the critical path method, the Last Planner System, Gantt charts and Kanban.

q: Complete each statement about adjusting the schedule.

blanks.text: Shortening critical activities by adding resources is
Doing sequential activities partly in parallel is
Adjusting dates for limited resources, which may extend the critical path, is

explanation: Crashing adds cost; fast tracking adds risk; resource leveling may delay the end date.
